summary: Summarizes research results on applying network coding to Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) and Named Data Networking (NDN) and sets out the technical considerations and challenges. It is a product of the Network Coding Research Group and the Information-Centric Networking Research Group, and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of sending the plain puzzle pieces, you send clever mixes of them, so any enough mixes rebuild the picture. This looks at whether that trick fits networks that ask for things by name.

questions: what is network coding in ndn
how can network coding help information-centric networking
how does network coding improve multipath retrieval
what are the challenges of combining network coding and icn
subtitle: Combining smart packet mixing with content-based networking

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) and Network Coding are each powerful on their own: ICN delivers content by name with built-in caching, and Network Coding (NC) mixes packets together so that lost packets can be recovered. The RFC explores what happens when you combine them.
tldr.mechanism: The document surveys how Network Coding techniques can be applied to CCNx and NDN (two implementations of ICN). It addresses how coded packets should be named, how forwarders decide when to create coded packets, how caching works with coded data, and how to ensure coded packets are authentic.
tldr.outcome: This is a research report, not a standard. It identifies technical considerations and open challenges for combining NC and ICN, including content naming, transport semantics, in-network caching of coded packets, and security validation of recoded packets produced by forwarders.

today: RFC 9273 is an IRTF informational document that summarizes the state of research on combining Network Coding and Information-Centric Networking. The document is not a standard and does not describe an implemented protocol. Research continues in academic venues and within the IRTF research groups. No widely deployed ICN/NDN systems currently implement Network Coding, but the document is cited in research papers exploring the integration.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Information-Centric Networking (ICN) shifts the focus from IP addresses to content names. Two implementations dominate: Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) and Named Data Networking (NDN). Both use a pull-based model where consumers send Interests requesting content by name, and producers or caches return Data packets matching that name.

Network Coding (NC) is a technique where intermediate nodes combine multiple input packets into output packets using linear algebra over finite fields. This allows receivers to recover lost packets without re-requesting them from the source. NC is known to improve throughput, reduce transmission overhead, and enhance robustness in networks with packet loss.

The RFC combines both: applying NC to ICN enables more efficient multicast, multipath retrieval, in-network caching of coded packets, and recovery from packet loss without additional round-trips. However, the unique features of ICN—name-based routing, signature-based authentication, and sessionless communication—create new challenges for NC deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: ICN lets you ask for content by name, and the network caches copies. NC mixes packets so the network can recover from loss without re-asking. Together, the network could mix cached copies and send fewer total messages.

sections.title: Basics of ICN and Network Coding
sections.content:
In CCNx/NDN, a consumer sends an Interest packet with the name of desired content. Each forwarder checks its Content Store (CS) for a match; if found, it returns the Data. Otherwise, it checks the Pending Interest Table (PIT) to see if the same name is already requested; if so, it adds the incoming interface and drops the duplicate. If not, it creates a PIT entry and forwards the Interest via the Forwarding Information Base (FIB). When Data arrives from a producer or cache, it travels back along the PIT path, and forwarders may store a copy in their CS.

Network Coding works by encoding source symbols (original data units) using coding coefficients to produce coded symbols (repair packets). Block Coding operates on fixed-size chunks; Random Linear Coding (RLC) generates coding coefficients randomly. A receiver needs K linearly independent equations to decode K source packets. The key benefit of NC is that any K independent encoded packets (from any source or forwarder) allow decoding, not just the original K.
sections.plainLanguage: ICN forwarders are like smart post offices: they check if they already have the package, ask upstream if they don't, and remember future requests. NC is like making puzzle box covers that can be mixed: if you have any four different mixes of the pieces, you can put the puzzle together without needing the original pieces.

sections.title: Technical Considerations
sections.content:
Four main challenges emerge when combining NC and ICN:

Content Naming: Should each coded packet have a unique name that includes its coding vector and generation ID (e.g., /video/gen-1/vector-1234), or should all coded packets share a generic name? Unique naming allows exact matching in the PIT but requires consumers to know coding parameters. Generic naming allows consumers to accept any coded packet from cache but may not ensure innovative (linearly independent) packets.

Transport Semantics: ICN is pull-based: forwarders only return data in response to Interests. This prevents push-based code spreading. Forwarders must track which coding degrees of freedom have already been provided to each Interest so they do not repeat non-innovative packets. This requires state management, raising scalability concerns.

In-Network Caching: Forwarders cannot cache coded packets without verifying their signatures, adding computational cost. If multiple coded packets have the same name, mechanisms are needed to distinguish which one is in the cache and ensure no duplication.

Security and Validation: When a forwarder performs in-network recoding (combining received packets to create new coded packets), other nodes must verify that the recoded packets are authentic and have not been corrupted. Multi-signature schemes, key restrictions, or certificate chains can address this but incur overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: If you name every mix with its recipe, the consumer has to know recipes, which is complex. If you use a generic name, the consumer might get two copies of the same mix. Forwarders also need to remember which mixes they have sent so they don't send the same mix twice. And if a forwarder creates a new mix, other forwarders need to trust it is not broken.

sections.title: Research Challenges
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four major open research challenges:

Convolutional Coding: Most literature uses block-based NC, but real-time streaming often needs convolutional coding (sliding-window coding) where the encoding window moves over continuous data flows. Applying convolutional coding to ICN's hop-by-hop forwarding is not well understood.

Rate and Congestion Control: Adding redundancy via repair packets can worsen congestion if not coordinated. The RFC points out that congestion control for NC in ICN—where multiple paths and forwarders each decide independently whether to encode—is an open problem.

Security: In-network recoding by forwarders creates two risks: (1) ensuring that newly recoded packets are valid (addressed by multi-signature or hop-by-hop authentication), and (2) defending against cache pollution attacks where an attacker requests unpopular NC packets to fill the cache with them. These mitigations are emerging but not standardized.

Routing Scalability: To benefit from NC, consumers need efficient strategies for requesting innovative packets across multiple paths. The FIB and interest-forwarding strategies must be redesigned to support this while keeping the routing system scalable.
sections.plainLanguage: Streaming video often sends mixes continuously, not in blocks. Multiple forwarders independently deciding to mix packets might overload the network if they are not coordinated. Attackers could trick the cache into storing junk mixes. And making the routing system smart enough to help consumers find innovative mixes without slowing everything down is hard.

sections.title: Potential Advantages
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that NC and ICN are synergistic. NC enables multipath retrieval: a consumer requests content on multiple paths in parallel, and NC ensures that packets from any path are innovative (linearly independent), so the consumer recovers even if one path loses packets. This supports seamless consumer mobility: when a device hands over from one network to another, ongoing requests on old paths may arrive out-of-order or late, but any innovative packets still contribute to decoding.

With NC, forwarders can cache coded packets rather than full source packets, compressing the cache. A cache storing four coded packets might recover all eight source packets for a consumer. NC also improves privacy: by spreading requests across multiple paths and allowing any combination of cached packets to satisfy a request, NC makes it harder for adversaries to infer which content a particular user is requesting.

Finally, NC allows distributed recovery: if a consumer loses packets on one path, it does not need to re-request from the source; innovative packets from other paths or caches are sufficient for decoding.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask for the video on two paths at once and rebuild it from whatever arrives. If you move to a new network, packets from the old network still help. Small caches can store mixed pieces instead of full copies. Attackers cannot tell what you want by watching one path.
